concept.name: Swap spread
concept.definition: The difference between the fixed rate on a plain-vanilla interest rate swap of a given maturity and the yield on a government bond of the same maturity. It reflects the relative pricing of the derivatives and government bond markets, including intermediation and funding costs.
concept.intuition: It compares the cost of exchanging fixed-for-floating payments in the swap market with the government's borrowing cost — a gauge of how dealers price balance-sheet usage and of relative supply and demand in the two markets.
concept.mechanics: Swap rate minus same-maturity government bond yield, in basis points. Arbitrage links the two markets (hold the bond funded via repo, pay fixed on the swap), but dealer balance-sheet costs, repo funding rates, bond supply, and demand to receive fixed can push spreads away from zero; long-maturity USD spreads have been persistently negative in recent years, and the shift from LIBOR to risk-free rates such as SOFR mechanically lowered swap spreads.
concept.formula: Swap spread = swap rate(maturity T) − government bond yield(maturity T), in basis points.
concept.failure_modes: Spreads are not a pure credit measure: they move with repo funding costs, dealer constraints, Treasury supply, and benchmark conventions, so treating them as a simple risk gauge misleads. Negative spreads are not exploitable arbitrage profits — they compensate intermediaries for real balance-sheet costs.
concept.misconceptions: A negative swap spread is not a 'free lunch' arbitrage left on the table; capturing it requires repo-funded bond holdings whose financing and balance-sheet costs consume the apparent profit.
concept.example: If the 10-year SOFR swap rate is 3.60% and the 10-year Treasury yields 4.05%, the 10-year swap spread is −45 basis points.

citations.source: BIS Quarterly Review, December 2024 — 'Negative interest rate swap spreads signal pressure in government debt absorption'
